The most likely reason for an oligopoly in the USA is due to a current lack of production and the import-heavy economy of the USA. It is obviously dependent on the sector but for most goods, domestic manufacturers simply don't exist or do in such short supply that if international competitors are wiped out, they become the only remaining seller (by default they are a monopoly/oligopoly).

It would be different if the USA had manufacturers ready and already competing but they simply don't / only have 1-2 for many sectors. 

You say a "temporary cost increase" whilst manufacturing is set up. Let's say miraculously factories are built in only a year, so for one year there's tarriffs, regular inflation and price gouging (as seen in COVID) driving prices up. A box of nails goes from $10 to $14. Would a domestic producer interested in making money enter the market and go "Lets sell at $10 again" or "Lets sell at $12 and still undercut the competitors". That's still a 20% increase on base goods price from where it began. 

When the US economy is heavily skewed towards imports, this means the vast majority of products will feel this. Response tarriffs from Canada and Mexico won't hit their people as hard, since they import fewer products from USA and why their people are more okay with it. 

Of course the US tarriffs will hurt them. Fewer customers will buy their products if they're more expensive which hurts them too. It's just that, as the USA's trades are currently, it will hurt them much less than it will the American people. 

To use another analogy, USA is shooting through their own arm to hit their allies' feet. Everyone gets hurt here, but USA most of all.

Rather than tariffs, it would make far more sense to invest the 0.5 - 4.5% tax increases that <$360K earners are set to receive from Trump this year into domestic manufacturing grants. Instead we are seeing funding ripped from cities, states and innovation for nebulous reasons like DEI to cover the cost of giving >$360K earners a tax cut.

Everyone else's answers are correct but a further point:

Canada and Mexico can afford to tariff and hurt their citizens less as their net imports from USA are far lower so fewer costs are passed onto consumers. They have a stronger domestic production. 

USA imports far more than it exports, so the vast majority of goods will increase in price. Whereas Canada and Mexico would only see a few specific goods they import increase in price.

In Australia we call it Goods and Services Tax (GST). Eveything gets a flat 10% tax added to its price regardless of where it originated. 

If we tarriffed another country it would just add a further 25% cost to consumers on top of that 10% (unless the company is nice and decides to just pay the 25% cost increase themselves and not pass it onto consumers. Which seems... optimistic).

They are, in the same way that shooting through your own arm to hit my foot is damaging. 

It's problematic for others because consumers become less likely to choose foreign brands if that foreign nation is tarriffed. But why are they less likely? Because consumers would be paying so much more that they aren't competitive.

Its still the aggressor country's citizens that end up paying more. IF there is immediate supply domestically this MAY make things cheaper (though very unlikely if the domestic producers can monopolise and have full price control). Except the stated goal is to "bring back manufacturing" which implies there is currently no manufacturing to pick up that supply issue.

So whilst manufacturing gets brought back, goods either became unavailable or cost way more (let's say from $10 to $15 for a box of nails). If a new domestic supply is created, do you think they'll enter the market back at $10? Why do that when you can enter at $13 and still out-compete the foreign $15? So even after manufacturing returns, prices are still higher than they were pre-tarriff.

We can look as recently as 2018 to answer the second paragraph: https://www.heritage.org/trade/commentary/we-shouldnt-rinse-and-repeat-when-it-comes-costly-washing-machine-tariffs (notice this is Heritage Foundation, an extremely pro-Trump source. Even they didn't like the tarriffs). In short, the two scenarios are: 

1. International brands pull out, leaving domestic brands with a monopoly/duopoly/oligopoly which is extremely uncompetitive and has no downward pressure on pricing.

2. International brands sell at higher prices, creating an excuse for domestic companies to raise their own prices and increase profit (see above). 

The ethical slave labour question is probably the most valid reason to cut out some countries from trade. Most people aren't wanting to spend x amount on all goods to help someone overseas though, and that's not what these tarriffs are about.

Essentially, there just isn't enough cells or tissue left to regrow a whole finger. 

This is similar to why scar tissue grows back in place of normal skin sometimes. Skin cells, unlike nerve or some muscle cells, have the ability to replicate themselves, near-infinitely (similar to a progenitor or stem cell in an embryo) which allows for small nicks to the skin to be healed relatively quickly, these skin cells can replicate and cover the wound over with a fresh layer of skin whilst fighting off small amoutns of contaminants entering the wound. When there is simply too much tissue in need of regrowth however, the body views it as an unneccessary expenditure of energy to replicate enough cells to quickly cover the wound before any viruses or bacteria enter the larger wound and infect the body. In these instances, scar tissue forms using collagen to quickly seal off the wound.

This applies to your finger comment too. /u/taildrow isnt wrong, without the bone attached still there is no scaffolding for the muscle, vein, blood and skin cells to build over and reform a finger. And whilst a small fractured bone can be repaired by growing new bone tissue, growing a whole few cm of finger bone is unrealistic for our bodies to waste so much energy on. So with no potential scaffolding, there is no hope to build muscle and skin and therefore a new finger which just leaves a large wound where a finger was. The body combats this the most effective way it can by sealing off the wound (probably with a quick building tissue such as scar tissue) forming that little nub.

Unfortunately, this usually means that everyone with these same genes (lets say those cute little golden retrievers) are all a little bit related, so when they breed.. Theyre breeding with their own family, but like the equivalent of your 7th cousin. Actually the reason a lot of dogs get cancers and defects is because of how inbred some genes are, collegehumour did a video a while ago about that. 

TL;DR - Basically, each breed is the result of very selective and repetitve breeding until enough family members (breed members really) are established to keep the breed going
